lines.text: Guess: how slow does time have to go to watch light move? Let's start with one second. A kitchen. A window. Coffee on the table. A fly crosses the room, and it's over. You barely noticed. Now I'll play that same second again, slower, and then slower again. I won't stop until light itself is crawling.

lines.text: No camera on Earth could film all of this. So every picture here is drawn by a computer, from the physics. When a number was measured by someone, I'll say so. When a picture is just an idea, it will wear a badge. Ten times slower. One second now takes ten. A small hummingbird hovers at the window. Its wings beat about fifty times a second. At ten times slower, that's five beats a second. Now you can see them. Not a blur anymore, just wings, going up and down. The wings are doing all the work of holding it still. Each wing sweeps forward, flips, and sweeps back. Watch the wing tips: they trace tiny loops in the air. Here's why they blur at full speed. Your eyes blend flashes that come faster than about sixty a second. So fifty wing beats a second just smear together. But look at the fly by the cup. Even at ten times slower, its wings are still a blur.

lines.text: A hundred times slower. One second now lasts almost two minutes. First, a fly. A fly beats its wings close to two hundred times a second. Slow it a hundred times, and that's about two beats a second. A mosquito's wings beat about five hundred times a second. Here, that's five beats a second. You can count them on one hand. Now look at the tap. A drop of water swells there, heavier and heavier, until it lets go. It falls into the cup. It hits, and the water climbs into a crown. The whole crown forms in a few hundredths of a second. At this speed, that takes a few seconds. You can watch each point of the crown rise. Then little drops pinch off, and fly outward. The cup rings. The water settles, and the surface goes flat again. Still with me? Tap like and subscribe. There's plenty more where that came from. The cup sits still while all this happens. Nothing here moved faster than you could follow, once you gave it time. But the next thing happens faster than a splash, in a hot pan on the stove.

lines.text: A thousand times slower. One second now lasts about seventeen minutes. In the pan on the stove, a few kernels of popcorn sit still. Then one jumps. Its hard shell holds the steam in, until the pressure wins. It pops when it gets to about one hundred eighty degrees Celsius. The pop is over in about two hundredths of a second. Here, that's about twenty seconds. The shell splits, and the white foam bursts out. That crack you'd hear is the shell giving way. One kernel becomes a fluffy cloud, many times its size. The foam hangs for a moment, then settles in the pan. Over the sink, a soap bubble drifts, about as wide as an egg. Its colors swirl as the wall of the bubble thins. When it pops, the hole races around the film at several meters a second. The whole bubble is gone in about a hundredth of a second. Here, that takes about eleven seconds. And somebody across the kitchen has just clapped. How long does that take to reach you?
lines.phonemes: ɐ θˈaʊzənd tˈaɪmz slˈoʊɚ. wˈʌn sˈɛkənd nˈaʊ lˈæsts ɐbˌaʊt sˈɛvəntˌiːn mˈɪnɪts. ɪnðə pˈæn ɔnðə stˈoʊv, ɐ fjˈuː kˈɜːnəlz ʌv pˈɑːpkɔːɹn sˈɪt stˈɪl. ðˈɛn wˈʌn dʒˈʌmps. ɪts hˈɑːɹd ʃˈɛl hˈoʊldz ðə stˈiːm ˈɪn, ʌntˈɪl ðə pɹˈɛʃɚ wˈɪnz. ɪt pˈɑːps wɛn ɪt ɡˈɛts tʊ ɐbˌaʊt wˈʌn hˈʌndɹɪd ˈeɪɾi dᵻɡɹˈiːz sˈɛlsɪəs. ðə pˈɑːp ɪz ˌoʊvɚɹ ɪn ɐbˌaʊt tˈuː hˈʌndɹədθs əvə sˈɛkənd. hˈɪɹ, ðæts ɐbˌaʊt twˈɛnti sˈɛkəndz. ðə ʃˈɛl splˈɪts, ænd ðə wˈaɪt fˈoʊm bˈɜːsts ˈaʊt. ðæt kɹˈæk juːd hˈɪɹ ɪz ðə ʃˈɛl ɡˈɪvɪŋ wˈeɪ. wˈʌn kˈɜːnəl bɪkˌʌmz ɐ flˈʌfi klˈaʊd, mˈɛni tˈaɪmz ɪts sˈaɪz. ðə fˈoʊm hˈæŋz fɚɹə mˈoʊmənt, ðˈɛn sˈɛɾəlz ɪnðə pˈæn. ˌoʊvɚ ðə sˈɪŋk, ɐ sˈoʊp bˈʌbəl dɹˈɪfts, ɐbˌaʊt æz wˈaɪd æz ɐn ˈɛɡ. ɪts kˈʌlɚz swˈɜːl æz ðə wˈɔːl ʌvðə bˈʌbəl θˈɪnz. wˌɛn ɪt pˈɑːps, ðə hˈoʊl ɹˈeɪsᵻz ɚɹˈaʊnd ðə fˈɪlm æt sˈɛvɹəl mˈiːɾɚz ɐ sˈɛkənd. ðə hˈoʊl bˈʌbəl ɪz ɡɔn ɪn ɐbˌaʊt ɐ hˈʌndɹədθ əvə sˈɛkənd. hˈɪɹ, ðæt tˈeɪks ɐbˌaʊt ᵻlˈɛvən sˈɛkəndz. ænd sˈʌmbɑːdi əkɹˌɑːs ðə kˈɪtʃən hɐz dʒˈʌst klˈæpt. hˌaʊ lˈɔŋ dˈʌz ðæt tˈeɪk tə ɹˈiːtʃ juː?

lines.text: Now, someone claps at the far end of the kitchen. Sound is air pushing on air. Without air, there would be nothing to push, and no sound at all. In a room, it moves about three hundred forty meters a second. That's why you never see it travel. The room is five meters across, so the clap crosses it in about fifteen thousandths of a second. Here, that's fifteen seconds. There it goes: a ring of squeezed air, crossing the room. Imagine standing at the far wall. You'd hear the clap only when this ring reached you. It reaches the wall, and bounces back. That bounce is an echo. You use this trick in every storm. Sound covers about a kilometer in three seconds. So count the seconds between a flash and its thunder, and divide by three. That's roughly how many kilometers away the lightning is. But a clap is slow. Something on this table is much faster than sound, and it's about to go through an apple.

lines.text: Ten thousand times slower. One second now lasts almost three hours. A famous old photograph by Harold Edgerton shows a bullet going through an apple. That bullet flew at about eight hundred fifty meters a second. The apple is about eight centimeters across. So the bullet crosses it in less than a ten-thousandth of a second. Here, that takes about one second. The bullet is a small, dark shape. At this speed, you can watch it drift into the apple like a slow fish. The skin dimples. Then the back of the apple blows outward, in a spray. Pieces of the apple trail behind it, one at a time. And the bullet is already past. In real time, that was far too quick to blink. It's moving more than twice as fast as sound, so it drags a narrow cone of air behind it. Even now, a table a meter wide would take it about twelve seconds to cross. A bullet is fast. But out the window, something is about to be much faster.

lines.text: A million times slower. One second now lasts twelve days. Beyond the window, a storm. Lightning looks like it strikes in an instant. It doesn't. The whole fall from the cloud takes tens of thousandths of a second. At this speed, that would take hours. So I'll skip ahead, and show you the highlights. First, a faint path of electric charge reaches down from the cloud, in jumps. Each jump is tens of meters long. Each takes about a microsecond. Here, one jump lasts one whole second. Then the path waits, about fifty microseconds. Here, that's almost a minute. Look at how it branches, like a tree turned upside down. At last it touches the ground, and a bright flash runs back up the three-kilometer path. That flash travels up to about a third of the speed of light. Even at a million times slower, it takes at least thirty seconds to climb. And that's the fastest thing so far. But it's still not light's top speed.
